title: ORACLE-SWE: Quantifying the Contribution of Oracle Information Signals on SWE Agents
read_source: https://arxiv.org/html/2604.07789v2 (28 May 2026; 12,542-word article and appendices read, including prompts, result tables and limitations)
datasets: SWE-bench-Live verified Python subset: 353 filtered instances.
Defects4J is cited as related benchmark context only; no Defects4J, BugsInPy or SWT-Bench experiments.
task: Controlled oracle ablation of five agent information signals: reproduction tests, regression tests, edit locations, execution context and API usage. Injects each signal, pairs and accumulations into a SWE-agent prompt and measures issue resolution. A separate validation stage uses stronger-model-extracted signals with a weaker repair model.
input_setting: Issue + repository + injected signal. Reproduction oracle contains test source, selective command and F2P test identifiers, applied to the repo for iterative repair. Regression oracle provides command and P2P list. Edit locations come from gold patch; execution context from native/custom stack traces; API usage from added/changed calls. Oracle runs intentionally reveal benchmark ground truth to measure upper bounds; validation uses model-extracted signals.
author_relationship_evidence: The full paper has no code/data availability statement or author artifact URL. Searches of the paper text and web results for the exact title/arXiv ID plus GitHub found no paper-linked Oracle-SWE implementation. SWE-agent is cited as a baseline dependency; its public source is third-party baseline code, not the authors' signal-extraction or experiment artifact.
source_commit_or_archive: No author-linked implementation, extraction scripts, result cache or public signal dataset verified as of 2026-10-15. The paper describes rule-based extraction and includes prompt examples, so concepts/protocol can be understood, but code required for exact rerun is unavailable.
license: Paper is CC BY 4.0. No author implementation license because no author implementation was located. SWE-agent baseline has its own upstream license; it is not this paper's source.
exact_models: GPT-5-Thinking-Medium and GPT-4o for SWE-bench Verified
GPT-5 and Claude-4.5-Sonnet for SWE-bench-Live and SWE-bench-Pro
Validation stage: GPT-5 / GPT-4o pairing for Verified; Claude-4.6-Sonnet as stronger extractor with GPT-5-Thinking-Medium as weaker resolver on Live/Pro
GPT-5-Thinking-High used to judge 50 sampled patches for cheating in a manual validation step
weights_status: No fine-tuned weights. The paper uses hosted models; immutable model snapshots and inference code are not released. Local Qwen would be a different evaluation and would require implementing the missing five-signal extraction/agent wrapper, so it is not a drop-in evaluation path.
evaluation_route: Read full article and appendices. Reproduction would require benchmark task filtering, selective F2P/P2P test extraction, execution-context collection, patch/API-location extraction, SWE-agent prompt injection, and repeated issue-resolution runs (120-step budget; three runs for reported ablations). Paper reports the reproduction signal as the strongest single factor; five factors together reach at least 97% on four model-benchmark pairings. Validation samples 100 tasks per dataset and reports signal gains, with three repeats in stage 2. Reported API costs vary materially by benchmark and setting (individual table entries around $0.17–$2.18/task; these are historical paper figures). No code/model was executed.
blockers: No public author artifact, extraction code, processed signal cache or experimental outputs located; exact method requires substantial custom implementation, which is not authorized.
Original hosted model aliases are not immutable snapshots and the validation uses several unavailable/paid model APIs; a local Qwen run would not reproduce model-specific outcomes.
Benchmarks are SWE-bench Verified/Live/Pro, not SWT-Bench, Defects4J or BugsInPy; data construction and infrastructure are large.
Oracle-injected runs intentionally provide gold tests, gold edit locations or other gold patch-derived information; they measure an upper bound rather than a realistic stand-alone test generator.
No root-cause-label accuracy or causal taxonomy is evaluated. The five categories are information signals, not defect causes.
concept_fit: High conceptual relevance to test-oracle value and issue-agent handoff: reproducing tests dominate individual gains, and combinations can interact non-additively. The study treats F2P tests as an information signal, not as a method for generating high-quality concepts; it does not diagnose root causes. Direct use is limited because the oracle arm leaks gold test artifacts and the public source route is absent.
recommendation: Keep as supporting motivation for direct, high-quality F2P tests and for measuring test information in an agent handoff. Do not choose it as the next exact reproduction baseline: no author code/data route, oracle leakage in upper-bound arms, expensive hosted models and unrelated benchmarks. The much stronger practical fit for the current dataset decision is #74, whose public Defects4J CSVs/notebooks enable analysis without model calls. Do not reimplement ORACLE-SWE without an explicit later request.
supporting_locations: Paper Section 3: definitions and rule-based derivation for five oracle signals.
Paper Sections 4–5 and Appendix E: benchmark cohorts, model configurations, ablation and validation setup/results.
Paper Appendix G/H: example stage-2 injection prompt and stage-1 signal-extraction prompts.
Paper limitations: signal taxonomy is partly subjective and not exhaustive; validation assumes model agents can approach oracle-form signals.
Paper itself cites SWE-agent as the base agent but provides no author code/data availability link.
